paraphrase: Yoga is defined as the joining with Brahman of that special movement of the mind which depends on one's own effort; one whose yoga has this excellence is called a yogin, a seeker of liberation.

paraphrase: One who is joining himself in yoga is at first called 'yuñjāna' (the practiser); one who has perfected samādhi attains the supreme Brahman; if the practiser's mind is spoiled by obstacles, liberation comes to him through practice over further births; one with perfected samādhi, his karma burnt by the fire of yoga, is liberated in this very birth.

paraphrase: The yogin should practise celibacy, non-harming, truth, non-stealing and non-possession (the yamas) and study, purity, contentment and austerity with the mind turned to Brahman (the niyamas); these give special fruits to those with desires and liberation to the desireless; seated in a posture such as bhadrāsana, he masters breath, which is with a support (sabīja) or without (abīja); by withdrawal he makes the senses follow the mind; with breath and senses mastered he fixes the mind on its auspicious support (śubhāśraya).

paraphrase: The support of the mind is Brahman, which is twofold - with form and without form, supreme and lower; beings have three kinds of contemplation (bhāvanā): of Brahman (as the Sanandanas have), of action (as gods and beings down to the immobile have), and of both (as Hiraṇyagarbha has); the knowledge in which all difference has set, pure being beyond words, known only by the self, is called Brahman and is Viṣṇu's supreme formless form; since the practiser cannot yet meditate on it, he should meditate on Hari's gross form that is the whole world.

paraphrase: Viṣṇu's power (śakti) is threefold: the supreme (parā) called Viṣṇu-śakti, the lower called the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and a third called ignorance-action (avidyā-karma), by which the kṣetrajña power, all-pervading, is enveloped and suffers the pains of saṃsāra, and is seen in beings in graded degrees.

paraphrase: Fixing the mind on the Lord as the support of all powers is the pure dhāraṇā; one should meditate, absorbed, on his auspicious form - serene face, lotus eyes, Śrīvatsa, four or eight arms, yellow robe, ornaments and weapons - until the dhāraṇā is firm, so that it does not leave the mind whether walking, standing or acting; then one meditates on the form without conch, mace, discus and bow, peaceful with a rosary; then without the ornaments; then on a single limb, and then fixes attention on the whole.

paraphrase: A single continuous flow of awareness of that form, free of desire for anything else, is meditation (dhyāna), accomplished through the first six limbs; the grasping in the mind of the very nature of that (object), free of imagination, produced by meditation, is called samādhi.

paraphrase: Knowledge (vijñāna) is what leads to the supreme Brahman to be reached; the self, all its contemplations ended, is what is to be brought there; having done its work of liberation, knowledge ceases; the knower, attaining the state of that, becomes non-different from the supreme self - difference was made by ignorance; when the ignorance that produces difference is utterly destroyed, who will make the non-existent difference between the self and Brahman?
